title: Nepal’s Floods Put Climate Finance Shortfall in Focus Ahead of COP31 - Carbon Copy
description: Nepal’s Floods Put Climate Finance Shortfall in Focus Ahead of COP31  Carbon Copy
publisher.title: Carbon Copy
full_article:
Last month, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah used his address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) to highlight concerns shared across South Asia and the wider Global South. The August 26 disaster along the Bhotekoshi–Trishuli river system has killed more than 1,400 people, with thousands still missing.

A month after the floods, Shah told the UNGA that recovery could cost as much as 10% of Nepal’s GDP, or roughly $5 billion.

The scale of the disaster has again exposed the vulnerability of countries with limited resources to climate-related losses. Ahead of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye, it has also sharpened attention on Loss and Damage, a key element of the Paris Agreement, adopted by more than 190 countries a decade ago.

On October 22, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) provisionally set aside $21.6 million for Nepal, including $20 million for recovery and $1.6 million for oversight. It was the Fund’s first provisional allocation for a specific disaster, but only a small fraction of Nepal’s estimated $4.77 billion in recovery and reconstruction needs.

The decision followed weeks of pressure after Nepal requested urgent assistance on August 31. Harjeet Singh, global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign and founding director of the Satat Sampada Climate Foundation, welcomed the allocation but said the delay exposed the need for a permanent rapid-response mechanism.

“No country should have to endure a catastrophe and wait seven weeks, through historic letters and relentless pressure, just to unlock the Fund’s first-ever emergency meeting,” Singh said. He called for a system that could deliver support in days, not months.

Singh also pointed to the reluctance of some developed countries to let the decision set a precedent for future emergency funding. While they backed the release of funds for Nepal, he said, they were wary of prejudging the Fund’s longer-term model.

That hesitation reflects a wider challenge. Vulnerable countries need far more than one-off emergency allocations, but developed countries have been reluctant to commit to the scale of funding required. “Nepal needs billions to rebuild, and this Fund is responding only in millions,” Singh said.

For Shah, the disaster was also a question of climate justice.

“We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” Shah said, summing up the climate injustice confronting vulnerable countries.

Nepal’s experience is not unique. From glacial lake outburst floods and landslides in the Himalayas to devastating floods, heatwaves and cyclones across India, climate-vulnerable countries in South Asia, and the larger Global South, face a common question: how can they respond to mounting losses when they lack the resources to prepare for climate risks in time, and who should bear the cost?





A growing crisis and climate losses





The climate crisis is growing in the Global South, with disasters affecting communities from the Himalayas to the plains and coasts. Over the past decade, South Asia has emerged as one of the world’s most climate-stressed subregions. According to a World Bank report, more than 750 million people in South Asia were affected by at least one climate-related disaster over the past two decades.

Nepal’s latest disaster adds to a series of severe Himalayan calamities, from Kedarnath in 2013 to Chamoli in 2021, Sikkim in 2023 and Dharali in 2025.

Cyclones and rising sea levels threaten coastal cities, while extreme rainfall is contributing to widespread flooding in poorly planned urban areas. Beyond the loss of life, such disasters can damage economies and undermine development across South Asia.

A 2014 Asian Development Bank study estimated that, under a fossil-fuel-intensive emissions scenario, six South Asian economies, including India, could lose an average of 1.8% of their collective annual GDP by 2050, with losses rising to 8.8% by 2100. Repeated disasters also strain public finances, diverting resources from long-term development towards emergency relief and reconstruction.

For India, the costs of climate change are already mounting. The country needs funds to recover from damage caused by disasters and help vulnerable communities rebuild their lives, while preparing for the risks ahead.





Loss and Damage Fund: Promise Versus Reality





After years of negotiations, FRLD was established at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, and operationalised the following year at the Dubai climate conference. It was set up as a dedicated international fund to help particularly vulnerable developing countries address the economic and non-economic consequences of climate change.

Also Read: Beyond Compensation: What Coastal Communities Lose to a Rising Sea

While adaptation seeks to reduce future risks, Loss and Damage finance supports responses to harm that has already occurred or cannot be adequately avoided. This includes rebuilding homes, infrastructure, indigenous cultural practices and restoring livelihoods.

At COP29 in Baku, developed countries agreed to take the lead in mobilising at least $300 billion annually by 2035 to support climate action in developing countries. But this broader climate-finance commitment stands in sharp contrast to the limited resources available specifically for Loss and Damage.

As of March 2026, the FRLD had received pledges of just $822 million. The gap becomes clearer when set against demand. The Fund’s first funding round initially had $250 million available, later increased to $342 million, while eligible developing countries submitted requests totalling $2.8 billion — almost 8 times more.

Nepal’s experience illustrates the scale of the shortfall. The $20 million provisionally set aside for Nepal’s recovery by the Fund amounts to less than 0.5% of its estimated recovery needs — which is almost $5 billion.

Countries across the Global South, including African nations, also highlighted the limited means available with the Fund.

“The Loss and Damage Fund has received pledges of only around $800 million, compared with approximately $80 billion in adaptation finance flows,” said Labanya Prakash Jena, a climate-finance expert and Visiting Senior Fellow at the London School of Economics, highlighting the limited financial support available to address losses and damages. Developing countries are particularly vulnerable because they often lack the financial capacity to absorb the impacts of devastating climate disasters, he added.

Mary Kyanyi, Climate Adaptation and Resilience Fellow at Power Shift Africa, argued that developed countries must take greater responsibility for financing the losses caused by climate change.

“Countries like Nepal, which contribute very little to global greenhouse gas emissions, are bearing a disproportionate burden of the climate crisis. Developed countries, with their greater historical responsibility for global emissions, must step up their contributions to the Loss and Damage Fund. Their commitments must translate into actual funding that reaches vulnerable countries, rather than remaining promises on paper,” she said.

Also Read: As Nepal rebuilds, a climate-vulnerable nation tests the world’s response

Shah’s appeal at the UNGA echoed this demand for climate justice, which was acknowledged by outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, who urged the biggest polluters to take greater responsibility for the damage caused by climate change.

“Those who polluted the most – and profited the most – must do far more to repair the damage they caused. Polluters must pay,” he said.





India: Who Pays for Climate Losses?





While India is highly vulnerable to climate impacts, including risks in the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region that it shares with Nepal and six other countries, its access to climate finance, particularly for loss and damage, remains complicated.



India is one of the world's fastest-growing major economies, and its energy demand is rising rapidly. According to the International Energy Agency's World Energy Outlook, India will account for the largest share of global energy consumption growth by 2035 as its cities expand, industry develops and living standards rise.

But economic growth comes with mounting climate risks, from the Himalayas to the coast. A World Bank report estimated last year that India will need $2.4 trillion by 2050 to build climate-resilient urban infrastructure. An OECD estimate says India will need $7 billion annually to cover flood damage alone.

India's position in climate negotiations is complicated by its emissions profile. It is among the world's largest annual carbon dioxide (CO₂) emitters, but its per-capita emissions remain relatively low. India emitted 3.19 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2024, accounting for 8.27% of the global share, while its annual per-capita emissions stood at 2.2 tonnes. Its share of cumulative global CO₂ emissions since 1750 was 3.57%, despite accounting for about 18% of the world's population.

The question is how India can press for financial support for climate-related losses while navigating its own emissions profile and its role as a voice for the Global South. Experts say that the case rests not only on historical responsibility, but also on the scale of the risks the country faces and the resources needed to address them.

The HKH region offers one example. Global warming has accelerated glacier melting across the Hindu Kush, Karakoram and Himalayan regions, according to Saurabh Vijay, an assistant professor at IIT Roorkee, whose team mapped nearly 32,000 glacial lakes across the region using satellite remote sensing.

“Glacier mass loss is accelerating, while glacial lakes are expanding in both size and number,” he told CarbonCopy. Their research found that the total area of glacial lakes across the Third Pole in Asia — a high altitude region containing the world's largest repository of ice outside the poles — changed by about 5.5% between 2016–17 and 2022–24, with some regions recording growth of more than 20%.

Vijay said the expansion was increasing the risk of glacier-related disasters in mountain valleys, leaving countries including India, Nepal, Pakistan and Bhutan vulnerable. Such disasters can claim human and animal lives and cause extensive damage to roads, bridges, hydropower projects and other critical infrastructure.

India has begun taking steps to address some of these risks. As part of the national GLOF risk-mitigation programme, Uttarakhand has installed its first early-warning system for glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) at Vasundhara Tal in Chamoli district, which lies 4,800 metres above sea level.

Monitoring and early-warning systems require sustained investment, from identifying dangerous lakes to tracking changing conditions and ensuring warnings reach people in time. Vijay said, “Adequate financial support can help reduce these risks and limit the losses and damage caused by global warming.”

According to Jena, India should make its case for support by explaining its emissions history and climate vulnerability. He advocated for highlighting “historical and per-capita terms, rather than focusing only on the absolute volume of its current emissions.”

He argued that India should seek rapid-response grants for extreme events such as heatwaves, cyclones and floods, alongside access to advanced early-warning technologies and robust methods for assessing climate-related losses. Such support would help India respond to disasters while building the evidence needed to establish the scale of the damage.

“This support is particularly important for countries including India who face growing climate risks but lacking adequate resources to address them,” Vijay said.





Why Can’t the Rich World Pay?





The debate over Loss and Damage finance ultimately comes down to a harder question: who should pay, and at what scale? As climate disasters intensify across the Global South, vulnerable countries are pressing developed nations to help fund recovery from losses they did little to cause.

CarbonCopy earlier reported how India could mobilise domestic resources and alternative sources of capital to bridge its climate-finance gap as international funding falls short. But domestic resources alone cannot meet the mounting costs of climate disasters. How to finance climate action is inseparable from the question of who should bear the cost of climate-related losses and damage.

At COP30 in Belém, Brazil, the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW) proposed one possible way forward. Its study suggested that if the world’s most responsible economies contributed 0.08% of their GDP to the FRLD, the fund could mobilise around $60 billion annually, roughly 75 times its pledges at the time. CEEW said the proposed contribution floor would raise global commitments to 15% of the finance required, up from 0.2% currently mobilised. That would still fall short of the $400 billion a year sought by developing countries.

The proposal is not an agreed international commitment, but it illustrates the scale of the funding gap and how predictable contributions from countries with greater historical responsibility and financial capacity could help narrow it. COP31 will test whether proposals such as this can be translated into concrete commitments and whether money can reach vulnerable countries when they need it.

For Nepal, the stakes are immediate. The floods have left the country facing billions of dollars in recovery and reconstruction costs. Abhishek Shrestha, adviser to Nepal’s Minister of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, said the disaster should force COP31 to confront failures in the multilateral climate regime.

He described Nepal’s experience as “a defining testimony to the cost of collective inaction.” He said the regime had failed to phase out fossil fuels, provide timely and adequate adaptation finance, and adequately fund the Loss and Damage Fund when countries urgently need support.

Shrestha also called for a coordinated regional response to risks shared by Himalayan and downstream communities. He warned that hazards originating in one country’s high mountains can quickly affect downstream communities and economies across borders.

He called on Nepal, India and China to jointly map transboundary hazards, establish unified early-warning systems and integrate disaster response and adaptation strategies, with support from the international community.

“Adaptation cannot be pursued in isolation,” he said.

title: German climber dies on Nepal’s Ama Dablam mountain - The Straits Times
description: German climber dies on Nepal’s Ama Dablam mountain  The Straits Times
publisher.title: The Straits Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU – A German climber died after a fall while descending from the summit of a Himalayan peak in north-east Nepal, a hiking company official said on Oct 26.

The climber, who had topped the 6,814m Ama Dablam peak on Oct 25, fell some 1,500m on his way back down from the summit and died on Oct 26, Gokul Thapa, head of the Real Himalaya company, which provided local logistics to him, said.

“His body was recovered by a search team today itself,” Thapa told Reuters from Lukla, gateway to the mountainous region.

Ama Dablam is a popular mountain among climbers in Solukhumbu district, home to the world’s tallest peak, Mount Everest.

Last week, two Japanese climbers died on another peak in west Nepal.

Thapa said the body of the German climber had been picked up from the mountain and would be carried by a helicopter to a hospital in Kathmandu for a post mortem examination.

More than 300 mountaineers have received permits to climb Ama Dablam during the current September-November Autumn climbing season.

Earlier this year, 10 climbers including a noted Nepali-British climber died on a mountain in Pakistan . REUTERS

title: Recovery work continues in Nepal 2 months after disaster - NHKニュース
description: Recovery work continues in Nepal 2 months after disaster  NHKニュース
publisher.title: NHKニュース
full_article:
Two months after catastrophic floods and mudslides hit the Nepal-China border, reconstruction from the mudslides and flooding continues. A United Nations official working in the affected area in Nepal says securing housing and helping people rebuild their lives are among the most pressing challenges.

The Nepali military has installed a temporary bridge over a river to restore a vital road link washed away in the flooding. It will enable relief supplies to be delivered by vehicle.

The government plans to move affected communities to safer, higher ground. It's preparing 20 locations for temporary housing.

The August 26 disaster left 1,457 people dead in Nepal. More than 5,200 people remain unaccounted for. On China's side, the country's media reports 43 people dead and at least 510 unaccounted for.

Sarah-Yen Stemmler, a humanitarian response and recovery specialist at the International Organization for Migration, says thousands of people are still living in temporary shelters.

"What is important to note is that winter is approaching and temperatures are dropping," she said. "So it is a priority to move people from tents and from temporary shelters to more durable, weather-appropriate shelter solutions."

Stemmler added that medical personnel and healthcare facilities have also been

affected, raising concerns about outbreaks of infectious diseases. She emphasized the importance of continued global support.

Reconstruction costs are estimated at more than 4.7 billion dollars. Nepal's disaster authorities say the work will take about three years to complete.

title: Nepal calls for global cooperation at COP17 to protect Himalayan ecosystems - The Climate Watch
description: Nepal calls for global cooperation at COP17 to protect Himalayan ecosystems  The Climate Watch
publisher.title: The Climate Watch
full_article:
Nepal’s Living Sagarmatha strategy outlines $4.08 billion in investment needs over a decade, linking biodiversity conservation, disaster preparedness and resilient livelihoods across mountain communities.

Nepal has urged the international community to turn environmental commitments into practical support, warning that mountain communities cannot tackle biodiversity loss alone as climate change threatens fragile Himalayan ecosystems.

Speaking at a side event on Monday morning at COP17, the UN biodiversity conference, Deepak Jnawali called for stronger cooperation across borders. Jnawali is Nepal’s national focal point for the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and a joint secretary at the Ministry of Forests and Environment.

“Mountain communities are on the frontline, but they cannot carry this burden alone. Now we need global cooperation,” he said.

He called for sharing technology, knowledge and financial resources to protect mountain ecosystems and strengthen communities’ ability to respond to climate impacts.

Recent floods underline mountain risks

Nepal’s appeal comes as the country recovers from devastating mountain disasters.

On 26 August, a catastrophic debris flow and flood struck near the Nepal-China border, damaging settlements, roads, bridges and hydropower infrastructure downstream. The US Geological Survey’s preliminary assessment described the likely trigger as a rapid slope failure involving a glacier, with floodwaters and debris travelling nearly 100 kilometres along the Lende Khola and Trishuli rivers.

In its 11 October coverage, the Associated Press reported that the August disaster had killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Authorities had ended the main search-and-rescue operation and shifted to recovery, with officials estimating reconstruction needs at approximately US$4.77 billion.

A slide at a COP17 session in Yerevan on 26 October presents recommendations on linking biodiversity and climate action, including a proposed coalition of champion countries to raise the profile of mountain ecosystems. Photo: Sohanur Rahman / The Climate Watch

On 11 October, another flash flood hit Gorkha district along the Budhi Gandaki River. It damaged homes, bridges and riverside infrastructure, with at least five people reported missing. Authorities evacuated residents and warned downstream communities to move to safer ground.

The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said a landslide-dam breach may have triggered the October flood. Its preliminary assessment underscores the importance of distinguishing between different mountain hazards rather than treating every glacier-related disaster as a glacial lake outburst.

Together, the events underline the need to monitor unstable mountain slopes, glaciers and rivers, strengthen early-warning systems and improve cross-border information sharing. They do not, by themselves, establish the extent to which climate change contributed to either disaster.

International recovery support is beginning to emerge. Reuters reported on 23 October that Nepal would receive US$20 million from the UN climate loss and damage fund following the August flood. The announcement concerns disaster recovery support, a distinct financing need from the long-term investment required to protect biodiversity.

Living Sagarmatha strategy

Jnawali highlighted ‘Living Sagarmatha: Nepal Mountain Resilience Strategy’, saying it has strong synergies with the three Rio Conventions, which address biodiversity, climate change and desertification.

He said the framework aligns with Nepal’s commitments under the Paris Agreement, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. It also emphasises social inclusion, Indigenous knowledge and youth engagement.

Unveiled in January 2026, the strategy identifies 35 priority interventions, with estimated investment needs of US$4.08 billion over a decade. Its priorities bring together ecosystem protection and restoration, glacier and water-system monitoring, disaster preparedness and resilient livelihoods.

Proposed activities range from sustainable forest management and early-warning systems to mountain agriculture, medicinal herb production, nature-based tourism and renewable energy. The investment estimate sets out the scale of resources needed; it does not represent funding already secured.

Mountains in focus

The side event formed part of Mountain Ecosystems Day on 26 October at the GBF Pavilion in the Blue Zone. UNEP’s outline for the day identified finance, science, Indigenous and local knowledge, regional cooperation and implementation of the global biodiversity framework as central themes.

Mountains connect countries through shared ecosystems and river basins, supporting water supplies, food systems and livelihoods far downstream. Cooperation on research, glacier monitoring, conservation and early-warning systems could therefore benefit communities across national borders.

For Nepal, the challenge is to translate recognition of these shared benefits into sustained international support for the people who live in and manage mountain landscapes.

Linking biodiversity and climate action

Restoring mountain forests and watersheds can protect habitats while strengthening water security, supporting livelihoods and reducing exposure to some environmental hazards.

Such nature-based solutions could connect implementation of the Kunming-Montreal framework with the Global Goal on Adaptation, which guides international efforts to strengthen resilience to climate change. Mountain ecosystems could also provide a practical focus for a proposed joint work programme intended to improve coordination between biodiversity and climate action.

Ecosystem restoration, however, needs to accompany hazard monitoring, early warnings and safer infrastructure planning in areas exposed to destructive floods and slope failures.

One policy option raised during the session was a coalition of champion countries and regions to advocate for mountain ecosystems. Such a grouping could raise their political profile and encourage stronger integration into the work of both the CBD and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. It is not an agreed COP17 outcome.

Next: Nepal’s national biodiversity plan

Nepal’s wider biodiversity agenda comes into focus on Tuesday. The Government of Nepal and the UN Development Programme will hold a panel titled “Nepal’s Biodiversity Vision: Turning Ambition to Action” at the UN Pavilion in the Blue Zone on 27 October, from 18:15 to 20:00.

The discussion will examine implementation of Nepal’s National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2026–2030, including sustainable finance, measurable results, Indigenous knowledge and rights, and youth participation. It will bring together government representatives, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, youth, and conservation and development partners.

For Nepal’s mountain communities, the test is whether global commitments bring predictable finance and accessible technology, and give them a meaningful role in deciding how that support is used.

title: Nepal, India to discuss border security at annual meeting this week - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal, India to discuss border security at annual meeting this week  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The chiefs of Nepal’s and India’s paramilitary forces will meet in Kathmandu this week for the 10th annual coordination meeting between Nepal’s Armed Police Force (APF) and India’s Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB), with border security and cross-border crime among the key issues on the agenda.

Narayan Dutta Poudyal, inspector general of the APF, and his Indian counterpart, Sanjay Singhal, director general of the SSB, will lead their respective delegations at the three-day meeting, which begins on Tuesday and concludes on Thursday with the signing of agreed minutes, APF officials said.

During his visit, Singhal will also pay courtesy calls on Home Minister Sudan Gurung, home secretary Kedarnath Sharma and other officials.

The meeting will cover a range of security concerns, including the movement of third-country nationals, boundary-related issues, human trafficking, cross-border criminal activities and coordination between the two forces in border areas, a senior APF official said.

Other areas of cooperation include joint border patrols, boundary pillar maintenance, disaster preparedness and response, action against illicit substances, a review of previous agreements, inter-agency coordination and future cooperation plans.

Officials said the two sides would discuss ways to strengthen coordinated border management, prevent transnational crime and improve real-time intelligence sharing along the 1,751-kilometre open Nepal-India border.

At the previous meeting, both sides expressed concern about the movement of third-country nationals through border areas and agreed to monitor their movement across the frontier.

“The Indian side raised concerns about the movement of Chinese and Pakistani nationals through Nepali border areas. We also shared our concerns about the movement of Rohingya refugees and Bangladeshi nationals. However, such movement has slowed down recently,” an official said.

Officials from various ministries and departments will also take part in the meeting. The annual coordination mechanism was established in 2012, although meetings have been interrupted by various circumstances, including the Covid-19 pandemic.

Nepal and India share an open border that facilitates the movement of people and goods but also poses challenges involving human trafficking, drug smuggling, customs evasion, illegal trade and the movement of third-country nationals.

“Given the close social, economic and cultural ties between Nepal and India, the open border facilitates the movement of people and goods but also presents challenges related to human trafficking, drug smuggling, customs evasion, illegal trade and the movement of third-country nationals,” a home ministry official said. “The coordination meeting provides an opportunity for both sides to review emerging security concerns, assess progress on previous agreements and develop practical measures to improve border management while facilitating legitimate cross-border movement.”

The two sides are also expected to discuss corruption, drug trafficking, customs evasion and smuggling, along with joint patrols and the maintenance of boundary pillars.

The APF has established 244 outposts along Nepal’s border with India, while India operates more than 400 posts. The two forces also cooperate in repairing and maintaining boundary pillars, including in the Kalapani area of Darchula and Susta in Nawalparasi West.

Nepal is expected to seek greater Indian cooperation in tackling drug trafficking and the smuggling of goods across the border, as well as more effective information-sharing mechanisms to address these problems.

Joint responses to natural disasters, preparing personnel for emergencies affecting both sides of the border, and efforts to combat the trafficking of drugs, alcohol and other substances are also on the agenda.

title: Xtreme is betting on Nepali sport. It’s helping both — for now - The Kathmandu Post
description: Xtreme is betting on Nepali sport. It’s helping both — for now  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
When Lokesh Bam was unveiled on October 4 as one of nine national cricketers sponsored by Xtreme Energy Drink, he didn’t know until that day that eight others would join him on stage.

“This kind of sponsorship is what helps players,” Bam told the Post. “I think this is a result of the success Nepali cricket has achieved.”

Bam acknowledged that Nepali cricketers earn a decent salary compared to athletes in other sports in the country. Nepali men’s cricketers earn between Rs35,000 and Rs150,000 per month based on their categories. They earn an extra fee of Rs10,000 per match for Twenty20 International matches and Rs15,000 per match for One Day International matches.

“But it is still low when compared to what cricketers earn in other countries,” he said. “And this gap is filled by sponsorships.”

How much that gap-filler is worth is something neither the players nor the brand is willing to say.

Launched five years ago by Agro Thai Foods Pvt Ltd — which was registered with the Office of Company Registrar in December 2019 — Xtreme now appears on the national men’s cricket team’s sleeve, on the front of seven of the eight Nepal Premier League jerseys, the country’s first franchise volleyball league, and, as of this month, on nine of its best-known cricketers. Every announcement has carried the same line: amount not disclosed.

Xtreme Energy Drink is also one of the leading advertisers in publications owned by Kantipur Media Group, including Kantipur Daily and Kantipur Television.

Players and administrators say the money from Xtreme has been welcome in the sports sector, long short of financial and institutional backing. Besides Xtreme, the company makes Max Tiger Energy Drink, Bam Bam, and Jelly Juice, and has also signed sports figures to endorse them. Max Tiger is advertised with Dipendra Singh Airee, the all-rounder nicknamed ‘The Tiger’. Diwiz Piya, coach and manager of Nepal’s MMA star Rabindra Dhant, endorses Bam Bam.

A board of Dipendra Singh Airee-endorsed Max Tiger, another energy drink under Agro Thai Foods, seen in Maikhola, Ilam. Nayak Paudel/TKP

“The amount under which we reach an agreement with athletes or teams definitely compensates for the stature of the respective individual or organisation,” said Soniya Rana, business head of Xtreme. “If you only look at the men’s cricketers, we were not only planning to sponsor nine, but the whole squad travelling to Oman for the ongoing ICC CWC League 2 tri-series.”

Xtreme came close to a similar sweep of the NPL team sponsorships. Except for Sudurpaschim Royals, which is sponsored by Red Bull, the other seven franchises (Biratnagar Kings, Janakpur Bolts, Kathmandu Gorkhas, Lumbini Lions, Chitwan Rhinos, Pokhara Avengers and Karnali Yaks) will wear Xtreme at the centre of their jerseys in the league’s third season, which begins on October 26.

“The other team had already reached a deal with other brands before we could get them,” Rana said. “We wanted to have all the teams wear our logos up front.”

Xtreme is not the only brand that wants to be seen. Still, it has come to dominate sports sponsorship in Nepal, with deals in volleyball, football, and esports. NPL franchise executives say few Nepali brands can match what Xtreme spends.

“In the first season, searching for sponsorships was like being in a fish market,” said Niroj Khatiwada, chief executive officer of Janakpur Bolts. “We also did not know how much to ask and expect. We learned something in the second season, and it was more professional. Coming to the third season, many things have changed and improved in the sponsorship sector.”

According to Khatiwada, the price of a franchise’s title sponsorship has risen by at least 100 percent since the second season.

“On average, a title sponsorship with an NPL franchise is around Rs20 million,” Khatiwada said. “Through the eyes of a franchise, we expect the overall sponsorship amount to help cover the cost of players, including overseas icons. For operational costs, the revenue from NPL is working out for now.”

Khatiwada said he expects sponsorship amounts to rise sharply in coming seasons as interest in the NPL grows at home and abroad. Asked whether Xtreme’s dominance helps the franchises, he said it cuts both ways. “It will allow franchises to bargain better. We can say to the sponsor that you gave this much to this franchise, and question why only this much to us,” he said. “I believe once multinational brands start searching for sponsorship slots in the NPL, this sponsorship race will be different than it is now.”

Former sports officials say brands have long competed to sponsor Nepali sport.

“Private entities have always wanted to sponsor sports events because they see a good return from there. In the end, it is good for sports,” said Tanka Lal Ghising, former member secretary of the National Sports Council. “In my tenure, I also honoured those private sectors, such as Surya Nepal, Kelme and Rastriya Banijya Bank, for their contribution. Private sectors spend more if they are well recognised for their effort. It is something that is lacking from the current leadership of NSC.”

With seven of eight franchises carrying Xtreme’s can and name on their chests, the drink will be on screen whenever a player bowls, fields or bats. For the company’s executives, that is exactly the point.

A view of the Balkhu-Tribhuvan University road section is filled with Xtreme Energy Drink’s advertisement gates. Hemanta Shrestha/TKP

“The way we are sponsoring every possible sector and event is to make the public aware of Xtreme,” Rana said. “It is what marketing is all about. The more people see Xtreme’s advertisements, the more they get keen on the product.”

There are some signs it is working.

“There were times when people used to seek only Red Bull,” said a receptionist at Hotel Dhaka Topi Restaurant and Bar, inside Birtamod’s Heaven Water Park. “Now, people come and directly ask for Xtreme.”

In eastern Nepal, Xtreme’s flex banners hang in front of almost every restaurant and grocery store, from Tarai cities to shops in the hill and mountain districts.

Marketing experts say sports has become a major platform for brands to advertise in recent years.

“The viewership in sports is huge, and when brands spend handsomely, it benefits both parties,” said Punam Singh, vice president at Nepalese Marketing Association. However, she cautioned that a brand like Xtreme should plan for the long term.

“There have been concerns raised over Xtreme’s impact on health,” she said. “What will happen to the brand if the government brings stricter policies for energy drinks and what they can sponsor?”

Until a decade ago, Nepal’s sponsorship scene, including in the sports sector, was dominated by alcohol brands. After they were prohibited by the state — officials cited health hazards even though they can be purchased anywhere and there is no age limit — Nepali sports struggled for advertising money. Now, Xtreme is filling that gap almost single-handedly.

A shop in Chaitubari, Jhapa, with gates of Xtreme Energy Drink and Max Tiger. Nayak Paudel/TKP

In response to the criticism over high sugar content in energy drinks, Rana claimed that Xtreme is a quality energy drink and there is no need to be concerned about its effect on health.

Xtreme is not the only energy drink in the Nepali market. There is Red Bull, which is also a primary sponsor of the NPL. It has its loyal drinkers and remains visible in some sports events, though not as aggressively as Xtreme.

For instance, while Xtreme was expected to monopolise volleyball — sponsoring the teams of Nepal Police Club to the first edition of Nepal Volleyball League — it was Red Bull that bagged the deal with Everest Women’s Volleyball League. After two successful seasons, the league announced a three-year title sponsorship deal with Red Bull on October 18.

“It comes down to the individual alignment of the tournament,” said Snevy Chapagain, chief executive officer of the women’s volleyball league. “Looking purely at monetary figures is one thing, but assessing whether a brand’s long-term vision aligns with the tournament is another entirely.”

“In our first two seasons, we partnered with Vatsalya IVF because their mission directly resonated with women,” Chapagain added. “Securing corporate backing — especially from women-centric brands — is no easy task in Nepal’s current economic climate. But as women's sports emerge as a high-growth sector, we are seeing forward-thinking brands step up to invest smartly.”

Xtreme says it is not affected by any of it, that it believes in its values, and does not see Red Bull as its competitor. “If you ask who our competitor is, it is Surya Nepal,” said Rana. “We want to become the No. 1 industry and the highest taxpayer of Nepal.”

And the next big sponsorship target for Xtreme is the NPL itself. When Siddhartha Bank’s five-year deal as title sponsor ends in 2028, Xtreme plans to bid.

“We wanted to be the title sponsor of NPL from the inaugural season, but we did not have a proper team then,” Rana said. “Once the deal ends with the bank, we will be there up front.”

The NPL is broadcast on Star Sports in South Asia, except Pakistan, and globally on NetTV. Overseas players including David Warner, Andre Russell, Moeen Ali, Jimmy Neesham and David Miller will carry Xtreme’s logo to audiences well beyond Nepal.

For now, cricket’s administrators are grateful.

“The way Xtreme is leading the sponsorship deals, especially in the NPL, has raised the standards of Nepali cricket,” Paras Khadka, secretary of the Cricket Association of Nepal, told the Post. “In sports, players and teams need financial stability, which comes through sponsorship. In the case of Xtreme, it is also sponsoring domestic tournaments of Nepali cricket, which has been extremely helpful for CAN.”

Whatever one’s feelings about Xtreme’s extremely aggressive marketing might be, the company is ignoring the noise and says it is only getting started. “Right now, it is just one tenth of the marketing we are doing,” Rana said. “We will get 10 times more aggressive in the upcoming period.”

Whether Nepali sport is enjoying a commercial revival or putting all its eggs in one basket can depend on actual figures — something no one has yet put on the record. Rana is more matter-of-fact about it.

full_article:
For the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This new setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

The first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

Manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising

Forecast

A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

The Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Warnings

Authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their plans and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those currently in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Climbing teams

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they plan to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

Winter soloist replanning

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his plans.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

title: Climbers Find New Alpine Lines on Remote Peaks in Nepal - Gripped Climbing Magazine
description: Climbers Find New Alpine Lines on Remote Peaks in Nepal  Gripped Climbing Magazine
publisher.title: Gripped Climbing Magazine
full_article:
Swedish mountaineer Fredrik Sträng and Norwegian climber Sindre Kolbjørnsgard have claimed three first ascents in the remote Humla region of northwestern Nepal, including a technical mixed route graded up to M6 on a spectacular 5,337-metre peak. The pair reached the summit on October 18, 2026, after an expedition nearly derailed by heavy snowfall.

Gripped has been following Sträng’s expedition in recent weeks, the climbs offer a glimpse of a different kind of Himalayan mountaineering that seeks new routes and extends the possibilities for climbers in remote regions, without the extreme altitudes and commercial pressures associated with the world’s highest peaks.

The team’s original objective was an unclimbed mountain in the Nyalu Himal, but a snowstorm beginning September 24 dumped an estimated two metres of snow in parts of the region, making the approach across Nyalu La pass impractical. Rather than abandon the expedition, the climbers turned their attention to previously undocumented peaks accessible from their base camp near Phendol Kermi.

The standout objective was a striking, tooth-shaped summit the pair have provisionally named Daara Peak. Its north face offered a five-pitch technical line through loose rock, steep granite and a snow-filled couloir, followed by an exposed ridge leading to an eight-metre rock pinnacle at the summit. Their first attempt ended in retreat as snowfall worsened, but a clear weather window allowed them to return and complete the climb.

“The exposure was incredible,” Sträng said. “On one side, the mountain dropped away for hundreds of metres. On the other, the terrain fell away towards the valley far below. The final tooth looked almost impossible to climb from a distance, but incredibly, we managed to place protection all the way to the summit.”

The team believes the three peaks represent first ascents, although the claims remain subject to independent verification. Daara Peak is a provisional name and has not yet received official approval from Nepali authorities.

For Sträng and Kolbjørnsgard, the appeal extended beyond adding new summits to the record books. Their expedition also raises questions about the motivations behind exploration and the responsibility climbers have towards the places they visit. Sträng is developing Last of the Wild, a documentary series examining humanity’s urge to reach the unknown and whether every remaining wild place should be explored.

“Maybe the greatest achievement of future explorers won’t be reaching the last untouched places on Earth, but knowing when to leave them alone,” Sträng said.

The expedition highlights the potential for technical climbing and exploration at moderate Himalayan altitudes, where new routes can still be found far from the crowds, fixed ropes and commercial infrastructure of the major 8,000-metre peaks.

For climbers looking beyond established objectives, regions such as Humla may offer a different kind of challenge that younger climbers with Himalayan aspirations may find appealing. That being, remote mountains, demanding technical terrain and the chance to contribute to the ongoing exploration of the Himalaya. What’s more, opening up opportunities for people of this region.
